lesson_title: Body Measurements, BMI and Medicine Dosage: Maths at the Clinic
hook_text: A calculator says this man's BMI is 0,003. The calculator isn't broken — the units are. Here's the fix that saves the question.
clip_script: Clinic scale says 82 kilograms. Wall chart says 168. Punch it into the BMI formula — mass over height squared — and the calculator answers 0,003. A BMI of 0,003 belongs to a paperclip, not a person. The calculator didn't fail; it obediently cooked the wrong ingredients. That 168 is CENTIMETRES, and the formula eats METRES. Slide the comma: 1,68. Square it: 2,8224. Divide: 29,1 — now THAT sounds like a human. Check the table: 25 to 29,9 is overweight, so 29,1 lands there, near the edge. And know the formula's blind spot: it can't tell muscle from fat — a rugby prop can score overweight while lean. It screens; it doesn't diagnose. Now the part that really matters: children's medicine. An 18-kilogram child, 15 milligrams per kilogram — 270 milligrams. The bottle says 120 per 5 ml, so each ml carries 24 — the dose is 11,25 ml, in a real syringe, never a kitchen spoon. The 100 ml bottle? 8,88 doses — and medicine rounds DOWN. Eight full doses. Paint rounds up; medicine rounds down. Both round toward safety.
visual_style: A clinic wall chart and scale drawing themselves in chalk; the comma physically sliding across 168 to make 1,68; a BMI gauge sweeping to 29,1; a syringe filling to exactly 11,25 ml beside a wobbling kitchen teaspoon crossed out in red.
mood: Calm and caring with an edge of urgency, the voice of the health worker who checks the numbers twice because they matter.
pacing: A jolt on the impossible 0,003, unhurried through the comma fix and the category, slowing to deliberate care through the dosage steps and the round-down rule.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson — this is the maths that looks after people.
